blocks.text: Jesus’ answer to Thomas is part of a farewell promise: he identifies himself as “the way, and the truth, and the life,” and connects knowing him with knowing and seeing the Father. This passage should not be used to authorize coercion, domination, or violence toward other people. Its “I am” language should also be read in its immediate setting rather than treated as a single formula with one fixed meaning. Later in the chapter, “the Father is greater than I” belongs to Jesus’ departure, obedience, love, and return to the Father; subordinationist, incarnational, mission, and Trinitarian explanations are disputed interpretive readings rather than conclusions the verse itself settles.

Jesus promises “another Comforter,” the Spirit of truth, who will remain with the disciples, teach them, and remind them of Jesus’ words. Readers have understood these sayings in overlapping ways—as speaking of personal presence, advocacy, communal memory, and later Trinitarian reflection—but those interpretations should not simply be collapsed into one another. The related term Parakletos can name Jesus elsewhere, yet that comparison does not erase the different referents and functions in these Spirit sayings.
